newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GERMANY IN DANGER OF LOSING GRAF AND BECKER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GERMANY IN DANGER OF LOSING GRAF AND BECKER.

text.p: Steffi Graf and Boris Becker, who set off a tennis boom in Germany in the 1980s, could both quit the country for a quieter life because of the intense attention of reporters, fans, freaks and tax inspectors.

The jail sentence which a German court handed out to Graf's father on Friday for dodging millions of marks (dollars) of tax on his daughter's earnings is sure to spark suggestions that Steffi may move her home abroad -- possibly to a country with lower taxes.
"There are times when I've been thinking about it, absolutely," Steffi Graf admitted in November, citing New York as a possible alternative.

Last month Becker, who has also had problems with tax raids on his home in Munich recently, said he wanted to raise his three-year-son in the United States because the boy had almost no chance of a normal life in Germany.
"The price I pay for my fame and success is my private life," said Becker, who believes he and his wife, who is black, would lead a better life in a multi-racial society.
Becker, like Graf, enjoys spending time in Florida and could also move to the United States.
In the long term, Germany will suffer in business and sporting terms when Becker and Graf are no longer in the limelight.
Both Becker, 29, and Graf, 27, are edging toward the end of their playing careers. It is likely to be a very long time before Germany can boast such high-profile tennis stars again.
Their possible departures from the country and eventual exits from the tennis scene are likely to have economic implications for world tennis as well as their homeland.

After the tennis boom in Germany, the men's game brought two of the most important tournaments -- the ATP world championship and the Grand Slam Cup -- to Germany, where sponsors were keen to sign cheques supporting them.
The country hosts an array of big women's and men's tournaments throughout the year. If the bottom falls out of the German tennis boom, the world game is almost certain to suffer financially.

For many years Peter Graf refused to follow the examples of Germany's soccer star Franz Beckenbauer and Formula One driver Michael Schumacher by moving Steffi's residence to Monaco, Austria or Switzerland where taxes are not so high.
Under his former manager Ion Tiriac, Becker moved his home to Monaco for several years before returning to live in Munich where his present manager is based.
But last month he told German television he was very worried about his son Noah growing up in an environment where almost all of his schoolmates are white.

"We have a giant responsibility for him in that he grows up as freely as he can," Becker said. "At the moment he isn't free....It is difficult enough to grow up with dark skin if your friends are white and the society is white."
The pressure of the media, who followed Graf's trial intensely, is also a huge burden for both players.
Becker is also becoming more and more worried about threats against him made by freaks.

"Suddenly the crazies start coming out of the holes and start writing threatening letters," he said. "It is really bad and that is where I start wondering if it is still worth it, if the price of fear is not too high."
